title: On Being Shuso in 2020
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart takes up the opening of the 2020 practice period and the installation of a new Shuso, held in a emptied zendo as the community leaves its building. Kanho reads Blue Cliff Record case 14, Yunmen's "An Appropriate Statement," with the start of its verse commentary, and closes with Dogen's "Practice Period" fascicle from the Shobogenzo. Along the way, Kanho describes the Shuso role as a rite of passage with Zoom as a "sub hub," and recalls treating early practice periods as a challenge event and signing up for everything. Kanho names the suffering of COVID-19, racial injustice, and long food bank lines, then ends by saying the community will take up the paramitas as bodhisattva practice.

sentences.text: Good morning and a warm welcome.

In the Buddha's time, monks would remain in one place during the rainy season, the time of the Buddha, for mendicant ascetics during the rainy season, as large groups of people moving together might unintentionally harm crops and animals, even themselves.
So we are continuing a very old tradition.
Well, we did it.
We opened the practice period and installed Daikon-chan, Eshuso, exchanged, are partially scripted.
And yet, when they are spoken, they are very true and heartfelt.
It is very strange to do all that in an empty zendo, isn't it?
The building is empty.
All furniture is gone.
All big belts and all our beautiful instruments are in storage.
There is an improvised altar and we are here.
And I call that good.
This is all we need.
We do not need toys for our practice.
Doing a Jundo around the room so nobody sitting there may feel odd.
Though maybe we can think that the whole world is right here sitting with us and that by emptying out the building, we made room for them all.
Or maybe like in the sutras, the room was filled with devas, and invisible gods.
So beginnings and endings come together in strange ways.
The Red Cedars Zen community is leaving this building.
We are grateful to these walls.
They were good to us.
And yet, it is definitely an ending.
And here is Daikon-chan, beginning a beginning, starting his time as Shuso.
Probably knowing him, he has already planned out all his classes on the parmitas, the perfections, and that chuckle I just heard says, maybe not.
I hope and wish that he will enjoy this time as much as I did when it was my turn.
Being Shuso is very demanding.
And at the same time, so energizing because the whole sangha pulls together and moves forward.
Being Shuso is a traditional rite of passage in our tradition.
A senior student or priest becomes head monk and leads with the support of a teacher.
The practice period is about six to twelve weeks long, and a time of very concentrated practice.
Usually, it means that the Shuso is sitting in a room packed full of fellow students.
It means meeting the sangha and sangha members for tea to speak of life and practice.
This gives both the sangha and the Shuso a wonderful opportunity to grow closer together.
The Shuso trains to serve as the central hub of the sangha wheel during those weeks.
But since this is 2020, Daikon will have a sub hub called Zoom.
And maybe the most frequently uttered sentences, maybe, "you're still muted" or "can you hear me now?"
So I apologize for any and all awkwardnesses that happened with our audio and video.
And maybe you didn't hear every word you wanted to hear.
We did our best, and it was an interesting experience.
During the coming weeks, you will have many opportunities to support each other.
There will be classes about the paramitas, retreats, and regular sits.
The Shuso will give away seeking mind talk, and also, he will express the dharma afresh from his view.
He will bring his own take on what the dharma offers.
Being Shuso is a great honor and privilege and gives the Shuso an opportunity for further development.
And by practicing and studying together, the sangha moves forward too.
To take hold of this spirit requires the sangha's full and unstinting support.
We usually have special intentions and aspirations for our practice in this time.
I remember in my early days of practice, I used to consider practice period a challenge event.
I signed up for everything and tried to do it all, be smarter than me.
And yes, we will all make special effort.
And then, it all unfolds, and we are almost surprised by what is happening.
The good thing is that with awareness, we can flow with whatever happens.
And we will be able to even if we utterly fail, we fail completely to make any of our commitments we so seriously put down on paper.
No matter what happens, we fully inhabit the practice period.
We will crash through all barriers.
Time is unfolding itself.
Even though we say, "now it is practice period," practice period is always.
Shusous cannot be Shuso without sangha.
It is a wholehearted effort.
It goes beyond studying.
It goes beyond teaching a class or even being a scholar.
Please consider the whole of the practice period to be one ceremony and let it shine.
It is like Zazen.
We don't do Zazen; Zazen does us.
We don't do practice period; the practice period does us.
Just like we don't practice Zazen to get something, we do not enter into practice period with the goal of getting something out of it.
We don't trade experience of Zazen for bodhisattva badge.
Our practice is not transactional.
We are not spiritual peddlers.
We strive to be present with whatever arises.
When times and conditions are difficult, we do not avoid these difficulties.
We turn toward that which is hard or painful.
In Zazen, we can become aware of a single thought arising.

We can bear witness to it and let it fall away without getting caught, without becoming entangled, without playing the duality games of right or wrong, no fixing, no choosing, no setting anybody's trade, including ourselves, no doing needs today take place.
Instead, we return to the breath and let Zazen sit itself and us.
This is not an escape from life, but a coming home.
Staying with this practice for however long it may take, and Zazen will take us to the place where we find "I am alive" and see the same aliveness in everybody and everything.
It is surprisingly difficult to find language to express us, or at least point at it.
The foundation, the grounding, the experience of life is in the living itself.
This wide open space in the heart, which is inhabited by life itself, is not shaped by concept or knowledge.
This is a tough teaching in the best of times.
Individually, we may be doing well right now.
I hope you're one of the lucky ones doing well.
But I must tell you, these are not the best of times.
The country, the world, our cities, our hospitals are filled with suffering.
COVID-19 has already killed more than 200,000 people just in the United States alone.
The Black Lives Matter movement must continue working toward racial justice in a racist system.
Unemployment is high.
People are hungry.
The lines at the food bank are long.
Political divides go deep, even splitting families.
I said before that when times and conditions are difficult, we do not avoid the difficulties.
We turn toward that which is hard or painful.
So, I would say our Schusel has his work cut out for him.
These are tough times.
Our practice does not happen on a mountaintop or in a vacuum.
It happens right in the middle of everything that is going on.
And yet, while in 2020, conditions are different in many ways, they also remain the same.
There's a qu'on that speaks to it, and I would just like to read you the qu'on and the beginning of the verse commentary.
It is number 14 of the Brooklyn record.
It is called, "Yunmeng's Appropriate Statement."
A monk asked Yunmeng, "what are the teachings of a whole lifetime?"
Yunmeng said, "an appropriate statement or an appropriate response."
*The verse commentary, an appropriate statement, leaping with life, the words are still in our ears, undeniably unique and lofty.
How utterly unique!
The onlooker has some part in it.
Why only stand like a mile-high wall?
Is there any such thing?
He wedges a stake into the iron hammerhead with no hole.
He misunderstands the words.
Old Yunmeng, too, is washing a lump of dirt in the mud.
He misunderstands the words.
Old Yunmeng, too, is washing a lump of dirt in the mud.
Shui, too, also is just passing on ornaments.
Under the jambu tree, I'm laughing, ha ha!*
This fellow has never been seen anywhere.
Only those on the same path would know.
How many people could there be who know?
This is just the beginning of the verse commentary.
I will pretty much finish up the talk by reading what the founder of our lineage, Dogen Zenchi, said about the practice period in the Shobo Genso.
I will be reading about the first page of it, Classical 79 of the Shobo Genso, "Practice Period."
In an informal talk to open the summer practice period, Ru Jing, my late master, old Buddha Tian Tong, presented this poem:

*piling up bones in an open field, gouging out a cave in empty sky, breaks through the barrier of dualism, and splash in a bucket of pitch black lacquer to grab hold of the spirit, to train constantly for 30 years, eating meals, sleeping, and stretching your legs.
This requires unstinting support.
The structure of the 90-day summer practice period provides such support.
It is the head and face of Buddhas and ancestors.
It has been intimately transmitted as their skin, flesh, bones, and marrow.
You turn the Buddha ancestors' eyes and heads into the days and months of the 90-day summer practice period.
We guard the whole of each practice period as the whole of the Buddhas and ancestors.
From top to bottom, the summer practice period is Buddha ancestors.
It covers everything without an inch of land or a speck of earth left out.
The summer practice period is an anchoring peg that is neither new nor old, that has never arrived and will never leave.
It is the size of your fist and takes the form of grabbing you by the nose.
When the practice period is open, the empty sky cracks apart and all of space is dissolved.
When the practice period is closed, the earth explodes, leaving no place undisturbed.
When the koan of opening the summer practice period is taken up, it looks as if something has arrived.
When the fishing nets and bird's nests of the summer practice period are all thrown away, it looks as if something has left.
However, those who participated intimately in the practice period have been covered with opening and closing all along.
An inch of grass has not appeared for 10,000 miles, so you might say, "give me back the meal money for those 90 days."*
So that was Dogen Zenchi about practice period.
The world needs us and the world needs our practice, because Bodhisattva practice is impossible.
And therefore, Siamul Soto Zen will take up Bodhisattva practice.
It will take up the koans of giving, morality, patience, energy, meditation, and wisdom.
Together we practice the paramitas so that one day our inner prison of self-centeredness will break open and set us and the world free.
I hope I have said words that might be able to support you in your practice.
If you find it is not so for you, please forget every single word I said.
Thank you very much.
May our intention secretly extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Illusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless, I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.
